flashcard_questions.a: Money borrowed and repaid within one year to cover day-to-day costs.
Money repaid over more than one year, used for major investments.
An arrangement letting a business spend more than its account holds, up to a limit.
A supplier delivers goods now and is paid 30 to 60 days later.
A fixed sum borrowed and repaid in regular instalments with interest.
Profit the business keeps and reinvests rather than paying out to its owners.
Money raised by selling shares in the business to investors.
Investment from a wealthy individual or firm in exchange for a share of the business.
Raising small amounts from many people, usually through an online platform.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the most a business can spend with £500 in its account and a £2,000 overdraft limit?
Why can a start-up not use retained profit?
flashcard_questions.a: It has not yet traded or made any profit.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the interest advantage of an overdraft over a loan?
flashcard_questions.a: The business only pays interest on the amount it actually uses.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main risk of relying on an overdraft?
flashcard_questions.a: The bank can withdraw it at short notice.

flashcard_questions.q: What does an owner give up by raising share capital?
flashcard_questions.a: A share of ownership and of future profits.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main risk of crowdfunding a new idea?
flashcard_questions.a: The idea is shared publicly, so it could be imitated.

notes: 15 cards: 9 term→definition covering every source on the spec (short-term, long-term, overdraft, trade credit, loan, retained profit, share capital, venture capital, crowdfunding), 1 one-step calculation on the lesson's £500 + £2,000 overdraft example, 5 single-fact advantage/disadvantage cards. Dropped 'personal savings' and 'cash-flow problem' as separate cards — the old deck already used the cash-flow one and personal savings adds little beyond the loan card.
